newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: LIFFE plans to grow LCE agriculture products.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE plans to grow LCE agriculture products.

text.p: The London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) is looking at developing new agricultural contracts after its merger with the London Commodities Exchange (LCE), top LIFFE executives said.
"There's a lot of potential for finding new agricultural products," LIFFE chairman Jack Wigglesworth told reporters at a press briefing during an annual futures industry conference here.

Wigglesworth said the merger, set for September 16, will give LIFFE "the broadest range of products of any exchange in the world." The two exchanges will by next year offer products in seven different currencies in money market instruments, bonds, equity indices and options, and soft and agricultural commodities, he said.

Futures exchange officials note that volume in agricultural futures is up substantially this year, due in part to increased price volatility which has sprung up as subsidies and price controls are scrapped. With world interest rates and currencies relatively steady of late, increased volatility in the agricultural sector has drawn not just farmers, but fund managers to the farm sector.
LIFFE is also looking at this trend. Phil Bruce, LIFFE's managing director of strategic business development, said the exchange aimed to promote agricutural contracts "as a new asset class."

Bruce said that the exchange would look closely at the LCE's existing wheat contract: "The LCE wheat contract is U.K. delivery only. We are continuing to look at that and ... considering if we can transform it into something with more European application."
He said there was also a possibility that LIFFE, through its planned link with the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) next May, could also look to the U.S. market for such a product.

The agreement between the U.S. and U.K. exchanges, announced in March 1995, initially calls for the CBOT's Treasury bond contract to be traded on the LIFFE floor, and LIFFE's Bund contract on the CBOT floor. LIFFE officials said there may also be a chance to do something with the CBOT with respect to agricultural products, including wheat.
"Maybe there's scope for us to introduce a contract based on European delivery. Maybe there's scope for Chicago to introduce a European-based contract," Bruce said.
Bruce said the main difficulties would come in pricing such a contract, given complicated European Union pricing formulas.

France's Matif futures exchange, and Amsterdam's Agricultural Futures Market, have each launched wheat contracts earlier this year. But so far the exchanges have seen relatively low volume, futures industry officials said. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
